claims.text: FT Strategies has started a series, Demystifying AI for News Publishers, and the edition on liquid content by Sofia Giannuzzi is one of the clearest explanations of the idea the owner has read.
claims.quote: is one of the clearest explanations of the idea I have read

claims.text: The guide defines liquid content as content that primarily consists of datafied components, or atomic objects, such as quotes, events or dates, rather than information already synthesised into an article, podcast or video segment.
claims.quote: today publishers mould content like clay into a finished product and let it dry, and liquid content keeps the clay wet

claims.text: The guide is right to point at data journalism as the working model, honest about measuring a story consumed in ten formats and keeping a human in the loop, and right that structured content could be sold through pay-per-query systems with AI agents.
claims.quote: The guide points at data journalism as the working model the industry already has, which is right

claims.text: The ChatGPT infographic is faithful on the definition, the three is-nots, the drivers and the challenges, but three lines set as quotations are the infographic's own, not the guide's, and one changes the sense of the Digiday line.
claims.quote: are the infographic's own, not the guide's

claims.text: The infographic leaves out the guide's open questions on measurement and human review, the 32% figure on newsroom alignment, and its expectation that the change may take a medium or large publisher several years.
claims.quote: the 32% figure on newsroom alignment

value.unit: percent, the guide's figure on newsroom alignment

claims.text: If content is to be liquid it needs water in it, and the water is not the format but the reporting: the notes, the calls, the documents, the half-recorded interviews, the hypotheses, the facts with the doubts still attached.
claims.quote: If content is to be liquid, it needs water in it, and the water is not the format. It is the reporting

claims.text: Once something is clay you cannot ask where it came from; the owner wants a graph of claims with confidence, evidence with provenance, sources named or protected, contradictions kept as edges: a fractal semantic graph, or a story vault.
claims.quote: You can mould it again, but you cannot ask it where the clay came from, or which part of the shape rests on which source.

claims.text: The guide's call for a complete reinvention of newsroom norms is a known trap; the method already exists in decades of journalistic practice, and the owner would bring back the experienced journalists and give them the tools.
claims.quote: The more I think about this, the more I think we already have the method.

claims.text: The inefficiency is in the tools: the raw material of a story lives in a notebook, a phone and somebody's memory, and most of the value created during the reporting is thrown away at the moment of publication.
claims.quote: most of the value created during the reporting is thrown away at the moment of publication

claims.text: Liquefying the notebook means capturing what the journalist already produces in the way they produce it: handwritten notes photographed and transcribed, calls recorded and linked, claims extracted into a graph the journalist can see and correct.
claims.quote: Liquefying it does not mean asking the journalist to fill in forms.

claims.text: Building a custom interface has become cheap, so every journalist can have a desk shaped to how they work: their own contact book, their own view of the claims on their beat, tools that adapt to them rather than a system they adapt to.
claims.quote: So every journalist can have a desk shaped to how they work

claims.text: The right picture is not AI writing everything with the journalist feeding it facts; writing the article is how the journalist discovers the narrative, a feedback loop between gathering evidence and writing.
claims.quote: Part of the skill of a journalist is writing the article, because writing it is how they discover the narrative.

claims.text: The article the journalist writes is one projection of the graph and is theirs; other projections, audio, a briefing for another role, another language, come from the same graph, and a question the graph cannot answer is the next piece of reporting.
claims.quote: The article they write is one projection of the graph, and it is theirs.

claims.text: With a graph that records who contributed which claim it becomes economic to bring in a historian, a librarian, a data scientist or a lawyer for an hour or a story and pay them for their time and the credibility they lend, which accumulates.
claims.quote: it becomes economic to bring them in for an hour, a question or a story, and to pay them

claims.text: An experienced journalist told their organisation must reinvent its norms will reasonably hear a threat; the message should be that their work is kept and made better with technology and teams rarely affordable before.
claims.quote: we want to take what you already do and make it better, give you technology you have not had, and build teams around you that were rarely affordable before

claims.text: Turning an article into a podcast is not liquidity, but a finished article can be liquefied, and a publisher with a long archive such as the Financial Times is sitting on decades of reporting that becomes more valuable with every link; start with one topic.
claims.quote: I would not start by converting all of it. I would start with one topic and liquefy whatever it touches

claims.text: A chatbot on an archive answers from whatever it retrieves and the reader cannot see which claim it relied on; the interface is what gets built from a graph, and the difference is whether every answer can name the claim and source it rests on.
claims.quote: The difference is not the interface; it is whether every answer can name the claim and the source it rests on.

claims.text: Personalisation should be neither static nor statistical: it is the intersection of two graphs, the reader's, holding role, company, sector, time, depth and language, and the story's.
claims.quote: It is the intersection of two graphs, the reader's and the story's.

claims.text: Read literally, prioritising readers' tastes is the brief that gave us clickbait, and optimising what people click is what digital publishing has spent twenty years doing without serving readers or publishers well.
claims.quote: But read literally, prioritising readers' tastes is the brief that gave us clickbait.

claims.text: When the owner pays a news organisation he pays for its judgment, what it thinks matters, how it checks it and how it presents it; readers' needs should shape the projections, not replace the direction.
claims.quote: Readers' needs should shape the projections. They should not replace the direction.

claims.text: The move from print to digital went badly for news because most of the value went to whoever sat between content and reader: by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising, and the owner would rather not repeat that with AI.
claims.quote: by 2017 Google and Meta took 54.7% of American digital advertising

value.unit: percent of American digital advertising taken by Google and Meta

claims.text: A graph that names every claim and source adds ways of being paid that do not depend on attention: pennies per use, an agent paying per question, institutions licensing the evidence, and a share of every use walking back to the journalist and contributors.
claims.quote: a share of every use walking back to the journalist and to the contributors whose evidence the claim stands on

claims.text: Search engines persuaded publishers to make content indexable and then earned the advertising on it; structuring content for AI engines is the same work again, and the readers of that structure save money by having it, which is a reason they should pay for it.
claims.quote: Structuring content for AI engines is the same work again, and it has a value to whoever reads the structure.

claims.text: Start with one journalist: pick one topic and its reporter, capture their notebook as a graph they can correct, build them a desk, bring in one paid expert, publish their article and one other projection, measure, then liquefy the next story.
claims.quote: I would end with one journalist. Pick one topic and the reporter who knows it best.

claims.text: Liquid content is the guide's term and the clay image is the guide's; quotations are from Sofia Giannuzzi's guide for FT Strategies and through it from Digiday.
claims.quote: Liquid content is the guide's term and the clay image is the guide's.
